passages.text:
DO NOT OPEN is a collection of 10,000 NFTs on Ethereum, built with Zama's encryption. Each token is a cardboard box. When a box is minted, the contract draws a random number for it and keeps that number encrypted. The cat inside, its state, its five traits and its rarity are all worked out from that one number. Who holds each box is encrypted too.
Encrypted here does not mean hidden behind a server or revealed later from a list someone prepared. The number is a ciphertext on-chain from the moment it exists. The contract can still compute with it: compare it, cut a piece out of it, add to it. It does that without ever decrypting it, which is what fully homomorphic encryption is for.
So the game is about what you choose to find out, and what that costs you. Shake a box and you learn one thing about it, privately. Open it and everyone learns everything, for good.

The game has five counters. One rule tells them apart: what is about a box is encrypted, what is about a rat is not. Money crosses between the two at the bureau de change, and the amount shows at the border.
Dollars buy boxes, studio packs and rats; boxes and rats earn croquettes; croquettes feed the cats. Each card leads to its chapter.

Every box holds one of these. Ten breeds, from the everyday tabby to the glitch that almost never turns up; four states, only one of them fully awake; and a few surprises on top. Spin the turntable and say hello. And then the ones you make yourself with croquettes, from thin to huge, all the way to sick.
1 / 10

passages.heading: Tabby
passages.text:
About 1 box in 5
The classic. Stripes, strong opinions, and a firm belief that your chair is theirs.
The odds under each cat come straight from the game's tables. How a box lands on one of them is the next section.

The first time you connect a wallet, the game hands you a release form, Form DNO-1: the terms of play, eight short clauses. They say plainly what you are walking into. The contracts are experimental software: nobody has audited them, and a bug, an exploit or a hack could lose what you put in, without the creators being liable as far as the law allows. The website is only a window: your boxes, cats and balances live on-chain, so if the site breaks, nothing of yours is lost. Nobody holds your money for you, nothing is refunded, and none of this is an investment.

You initial each clause, one click each, then sign with your wallet. The signature is free and sends no transaction: your wallet shows a readable message naming your address, the version of the terms and a fingerprint of the full English text. The translations are there to read; the English text is what you sign. The signature is kept as a record of your acceptance, by the game's server when it is reachable, and always in your browser. Without a wallet, nothing is asked: you can look around the whole site, and the form only comes up when a wallet that has not signed it connects. You can close it to keep looking around, or switch to another wallet from it; any action you then ask for (a mint, a shake, a feed) brings it back until it is signed.

Each new wallet signs once, and a new version of the terms is signed again before playing on. To read the form again and see your signature, open the menu and choose Terms of play. On the test network nothing is signed: the form waits for mainnet, and a notice says instead what an update of the contracts keeps (your points, your whitelist seat, your X pass).

A box holds a single 64-bit seed. Its bits are cut into seven fields. Sixteen decide whether the cat is alive, asleep, a ghost or quantum. Five bytes are the five traits. The last byte only changes how the cat looks.
Encrypted
Fields of the seed
A sealed seed Open it 0x ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ???? Cosmetic Room Thing it broke Accessory Mood Breed State roll Bits 0 to 15. Sixteen bits decide the state: alive 70%, asleep 20%, ghost 8.0%, quantum 2.0%. The alive check compares them with 45,875 under encryption and publishes the one-bit answer. A shake can never return these bits. On-chain it stays like this: a ciphertext that reads as noise. The contract computes on it without decrypting it. Draw another seed

Keeping one encrypted number instead of eight keeps a mint cheap. Everything else is worked out from it when a mechanic needs it: under encryption while the box is sealed, in the clear once the box is opened. The app reads a seed exactly the way the contract does, so the cat you see is the cat the chain holds.
The rarity score is a weighted sum: three times the breed roll, the mood roll, twice the accessory roll, the broken thing, the room, plus a bonus for the state. A quantum cat starts 1,000 points ahead. The highest possible score is 3,040.

The owner of each box is encrypted, like its seed. That is not how NFTs usually work: an ordinary NFT says publicly who owns it. Here nothing does. Nobody can see who holds a box, or count anyone's boxes. The collection follows a new standard written for this, the confidential ERC-721.
Sending a box never fails because of who holds it. If you hold it, it moves; if you do not, nothing happens. Either way the sender and the receiver get an encrypted receipt that only they can read, saying whether the box moved, and everyone else sees a transfer that may or may not have happened. You find your own boxes the same way: the app reads the receipts that name you and decrypts them, with one signature per visit. That is what Show my boxes does.

Minting works on the same idea. It is paid in cUSDC only, and your browser encrypts how many boxes you want. You also pick how many token ids to hide that number among, from 1 to 10, and that choice is public. The first ids, up to your quantity, are yours; the others are empty boxes owned by nobody, and from outside the two look the same. More ids hide the quantity better and cost more gas. A mint that would pass the cap, or that your cUSDC balance does not cover, gets nothing and pays nothing.

The number of boxes sold is an encrypted counter, capped at 9,000 under encryption: of the 10,000 boxes, the other 1,000 are kept for the whitelist's gifts, minted free when a seated wallet collects its gift, never sold. Only milestones of the sale are announced: 100, 500, 1,000, 2,500, 5,000, 7,500, 9,000, the last one meaning sold out. The gift boxes count in none of them. Each mint makes public a single yes-or-no answer, whether the next milestone is reached, and anyone can announce it.

Some things stay visible, by design. A mint shows the buyer's address and how many ids it created, which is an upper bound on what they bought. A transfer attempt shows who sent it and to whom, as a maybe. And an action that has to become public (an opening, an alive check, a box put up for a duel, or a duel or an entanglement that goes through) shows that its caller held that box at that moment. An attempt by someone who did not hold it settles as refused and shows nothing about the box. Croquettes add one more: the app only feeds boxes you hold, so a meal, whose event names the feeder, shows a box you hold, even though the contract treats a stranger's meal the same way. Claims do not: the app always claims for whole rows of ten box numbers, yours among others.

This is also why the leaderboard ranks only opened cats, and the players who opened them: an opening publishes its opener, while who holds a sealed box stays hidden.
One of those public facts reaches further. Once an action has shown that an address held a box, the next transfer of that box from that address is certainly real, not a maybe, so the box can be followed to its next holder, and from there onwards. When you give a box away, you can tick "Send 3 decoys with it": three more transfers of the same box to random addresses, which move nothing but look like the real one, sent in a random order with it. Then nobody can tell which one moved the box, or whether any did. Each costs gas. Without decoys, keep a box out of sight by receiving it, or moving it, at a fresh address you never use to prove anything.

Every ciphertext has an access list. For the seed, that list has one entry: the contract. No holder is ever added to it, because an address on the list could ask the key service to decrypt the seed directly and skip the game.
Fact | The holder | Everyone else
Who holds a box | Yes, from their receipts | No
How many boxes an account holds | Yes, for their own account | No
How many boxes are sold | Nobody. Only milestones are announced
The seed, the state, the score | No | No
One trait per shake | Yes, free | Yes, by paying
Which trait a shake picked | Only whoever shook
Whether it is alive | Everyone, if the holder asks. One bit, once per box
Who won a duel, and one trait of the loser | Everyone
The winner's trait in a duel | No | No
How many times it was petted, and how many meals it ate | Nobody. Attempts are public, not whether they counted
How much affection that earned | No | No

Two consequences are deliberate. A holder who shakes often enough learns all five traits: a shake shows one of five at random, so about eleven cover them. What stays hidden even from the holder is the state, which is worth up to a third of the score, and the affection. And duels leak order: each one publishes which of two boxes scores higher. Putting a box up for a duel also shows that you hold it: that is how the duel shelf only carries boxes someone holds. That is the price of duelling.

Action | Who | Cost | What becomes public
Mint | Anyone, hiding how many among 1 to 10 ids | 5 cUSDC a box | The buyer and how many ids, not how many are real
Shake | The holder | Gas only | That someone shook, not whether they hold it
Paid shake (or a rat's sniff) | Anyone | 2.5 cUSDC, 70% waits in the box for its holder | That someone paid to shake
Collect shake earnings | Anyone, for the boxes they hold | Gas only | Ten box numbers in a row, not which or how much
Pet | Anyone | 0.5 cUSDC | That someone petted it, not whether it counted or what it earned
Alive check | The holder, once | Gas only | One bit, and that the caller held the box
Entangle | Both holders | Gas only | The link, and that both held their boxes. Opening one then opens both

Duel | The holder puts it up, any holder takes it up | Gas only | That the challenger holds the box, then who won and one trait of the loser, or a void duel
Open | The holder | 1 cUSDC | Everything, permanently, and who opened it
Feed croquettes | The holder | Up to 1,000 croquettes a day, all eaten | Who fed which cat (the app only feeds your own), not whether it counted or what it held
Claim croquettes | Anyone | Gas only | Ten box numbers in a row, not which are yours or how much
Weigh an opened cat | Anyone | Gas only | Its weight, its build, whether it is sick
Petting adds a hidden amount between 0 and 3 to a hidden counter, and nothing at all if the pet was not paid. So the pets anyone can see on-chain say nothing about the counter, not even how many counted. Past 10, the accessory turns golden when the box is opened, and a cat with no accessory gets a golden bell collar.

Every price is in cUSDC, Zama's confidential USDC: nobody but you can read your balance or follow your payments, and the amount you paid is encrypted like the rest. A cUSDC payment cannot fail on-chain: a short balance just moves 0, and the action then does nothing. A mint gets no boxes, a paid shake reads "not yours", a pet adds nothing, an opening is refused. Paying from plain USDC means shielding the exact price into cUSDC first, in public, and for a mint that amount gives the quantity away. Shielding a round amount ahead of time, at the bureau de change, does not.

Duels have a ranking of their own, in the leaderboard's Duels tab: boxes, not players, by duels won, then by fewest lost. The top three wear a rosette pinned to the front of their box, gold, silver and bronze, as at a cat show. A box can climb the podium and stay sealed: the ranking uses only the winners and losers that every duel already makes public, never who holds the box.

There are two ways out of encryption. A private decryption re-encrypts a value for one person, who must be on its access list. A public decryption publishes a value with signatures from the parties that share the key, and the contract verifies those signatures before it believes anything.
The contract never receives a callback. A reveal is a request on-chain, a decryption off-chain, and a second transaction that carries the proof back. Anyone may send that second transaction. Every request also checks, under encryption, that its caller holds the box; that bit is decrypted with the rest, and a no settles the request as refused, with zeros in place of the box's values.

On this protocol an access grant cannot be revoked. A design that put the holder on the seed's access list could never take the seller off it. This one never puts anyone on, so a sale has nothing to undo on the seed. What changes hands is the encrypted owner, along with what waits in the box: paid-shake earnings and croquettes go with it.
Mint Seed: the contract only. Owner: Alice, encrypted. The receipt: Alice only.
Alice shakes A fresh ciphertext holding one trait: the contract and Alice.
Alice sells to Bob She sends it. The owner changes under encryption, and the receipt, moved or not, is readable by Alice and Bob only. Nothing about the seed changes.
Bob shakes Another fresh ciphertext: the contract and Bob.
Alice tries again No error. She reads "not yours"; everyone else sees a shake, not that it failed. She keeps what she already saw, and gets nothing new.

Bob claims The paid-shake earnings and croquettes waiting in the box go to him now, not to Alice.
If you buy a sealed box, assume the seller knows its five traits. A few paid shakes before buying level that. And a transfer that names you is only a maybe until you decrypt its receipt: Show my boxes does it for you.

Everything in the game is priced in USDC, a dollar stablecoin, and most of it is paid in cUSDC, its encrypted form: nobody but you can read your balance or follow your payments. Here is every fee, who receives it, and what it pays for.
Players pay fees in USDC; they go to the collection's treasury, except 70% of a paid shake, which goes to the box's holder; the treasury pays Zama for decryptions and the servers
Dollars come in through four doors and almost all of them land in the treasury. The treasury pays Zama for the decryptions players do not pay for themselves (their free daily units), the servers that follow the chain, and the AI services behind the studio.
What you pay for | Price | Where it goes
Minting a box | 5 USDC a box | The collection's treasury
Opening a box | 1 USDC | The collection's treasury
Petting a cat | 0.5 USDC | The collection's treasury

Shaking someone else's box, or sending your rat to sniff it | 2.5 USDC | 70% to whoever holds the box, 30% to the treasury. An empty id has no holder: it still shows a trait, and the 70% goes to the treasury too. A power-1 rat gets 0.75 back from the treasury, in secret
Decryption credits, past the free ones | 0.01 USDC each | The collection's treasury
Buying USDC with ETH on the site | 0.3% of the ETH | The collection's treasury
A studio pack (AI sketches and 3D models) | 2 USDC (Starter) or 8 USDC (Litter) | The treasury, which pays the AI services out of it
Adopting a studio rat | 1 USDC, 3 USDC for an AI rat | The treasury
A croquette meal | Croquettes, not dollars | 20% to the treasury, 20% burnt, 60% back to the daily purr
Shaking your own box, the alive check, entangling, duels, sending a box | Free | Only the network's gas, like any transaction

Why decryptions cost anything: reading something encrypted takes work from Zama's network. The parties that share the decryption key each have to take part, and Zama charges for it, for every value read, from a tenth of a cent to ten cents depending on the plan. Checking the proof that comes with a value your browser encrypts costs five times as much. It charges the collection, not you. Shaking, finding your boxes, reading your own balance, the result of a duel: each one is a decryption. Minting, feeding a cat or sending croquettes: each one encrypts a value.

So every wallet gets 25 free units a day, paid by the collection, and they come back at midnight UTC; a wallet that has not played yet gets 16, enough for a first mint. Reading a value is one unit: a shake uses 2, and finding the boxes from a mint uses one per box number it hid among. Encrypting a value, like a mint's quantity or a meal, is 5. What your browser has read once, it remembers, and it is never counted again. Past the free ones, you spend credits, one per unit, bought at the bureau de change. Their price follows what Zama charges the collection in dollars, not the price of Zama's token, so it does not swing with the market. They are paid in plain USDC on purpose: a balance that falls short cancels the purchase, where a cUSDC payment would quietly move nothing. Making a value public, to open a box, settle a duel or announce a milestone, is 1 unit a value, counted to the wallet that asks first: an opening takes 2 to 5, a duel 1 to post and 5 to settle. Asked again, by anyone, it is free. That way nobody can post duels in a loop at the collection's expense. In the game, the Decryptions meter at the top right counts what is left (free today, plus credits): it blinks when you are running low, turns red at zero, and a click opens the bureau de change to buy more.

The treasury pays what keeps the game running: Zama's fees for every free unit, and the servers that follow the chain so the site stays fast. The rest goes to the project. Nobody can read the cUSDC it receives, the owner included: read after every payment, it would give away each mint's hidden quantity, and so who bought which boxes. The owner withdraws it at most once every 7 days, so it only ever learns weekly sums. An opening's 1 USDC fee waits until the opening settles: it joins the treasury when the box opens, and goes back to the opener if the box's entangled partner opened it first.

The game uses five tokens: ETH for the network's gas, USDC and CROQ, which are plain, and cUSDC and cCROQ, the same money sealed. A plain balance is public, like any ordinary token; a sealed one is encrypted, and only you can read it. To go from one to another, open the menu and choose Bureau de change: say what you hand over and what you want, and it finds the way and shows every cost before you sign. The rate and the number of transactions stay in sight under the form; Details unfolds the route, each fee and what becomes public. It also lists what you hold; sealed balances are decrypted on demand, for you alone, with one signature.
The five tokens of the bureau de change: ETH, USDC and CROQ are plain, cUSDC and cCROQ sealed, and the roads between them

Every arrow is one transaction; any other pair chains them, ETH to cCROQ in three. ETH can also land straight in cUSDC through the ramp. Each crossing of the border shows its amount; inside the sealed side, nothing does.
Some exchanges take one transaction: buying USDC with ETH (it can arrive sealed, as cUSDC), shielding USDC into cUSDC or unshielding it back, buying or selling CROQ for USDC, sealing CROQ into cCROQ or unsealing it. Any other pair chains these steps: ETH to cCROQ, for example, is three. Each step is its own transaction, signed one after the other, and in between the money waits in your wallet as plain USDC or CROQ. If a step delivers nothing, because a sealed balance smaller than the amount moves nothing, without a word, the bureau stops and tells you where your money is. ETH can only be handed over, never received.

Buying USDC with ETH costs 0.3% of the ETH, kept by the site. Shielding and unshielding are free. Every step pays the network's gas, like any transaction. A trade on a pool can land at a worse price than quoted if someone trades first: the slippage tolerance, 1% unless you change it (from 0.01% to 50%), is how much worse you accept before the transaction cancels itself, costing only the gas. The bureau also shows the price impact, how much your own trade moves the pool's price, and warns you above 2%.
What becomes public: plain tokens move in the open, so every swap shows its amounts, and so does every crossing between plain and sealed. The amount you shield or seal is public, and so is the amount you unshield or unseal: it is decrypted in public to be paid out, which is why those steps take a minute longer. Once your money is sealed, what you do with it stays private.

Decryption credits are bought in plain USDC only. So when what you want is cUSDC, from ETH or from USDC, the bureau can keep a share of it plain: none, 5%, 10% or 20%, the choice is remembered. From ETH that takes two buys on the ramp, one plain and one sealed, at the same fee; from USDC, only the rest is shielded. The bureau shows the USDC kept and how many credits it buys at least. The credits themselves are sold only at the bureau, in a window of their own to the left of the counter (under your holdings on a narrow screen), since they are spent rather than held: pick a quantity, see the price, buy. When the plain USDC is short, it sends you back to the counter to get some.

Croquettes are the game's money, and they come in two forms. CROQ is a plain ERC-20 with a fixed supply of 20,000,000: nothing can mint more, and it has no decimals, so one CROQ is one croquette. Being plain, any market can list it. cCROQ is the same croquette wrapped into a confidential token (ERC-7984): balances and transfer amounts are encrypted. The game only ever uses cCROQ.
Plain CROQ trades on a public market; wrapped, it becomes confidential cCROQ, the one the game uses
Crossing the border shows the amount: wrapping moves plain CROQ, and unwrapping goes through a public decryption. Everything that happens in cCROQ in between stays encrypted.
The whole supply was minted once, at deployment, and split like this:
How the 20,000,000 croquettes were split
Game reserve 10,000,000 In the Pantry. Pays the daily purr, and takes back part of every meal.

Welcome bags 1,000,000 In the Pantry. One bag for each box that can ever exist.
Market 4,000,000 Put in the public pool on its own, with no USDC, and locked there for good.
Treasury 5,000,000 Plain CROQ kept for events and more liquidity later; 500,000 of it went to the rats' pantry.

Croquettes reach players from the Pantry, the contract that runs the economy. Every box someone bought brings a welcome bag of 100 the first time it is claimed for: once per box, whoever holds it, so a second wallet earns nothing. Then each box purrs: every day, an encrypted amount between 0 and 4, multiplied by 2 for a Vet Certified box, collected up to 7 days at a time. An empty id, one a mint creates beyond the quantity bought and that nobody holds, gets no bag and no purr. Bags and purrs are paid into the box, an encrypted stash, and whoever claims receives the stashes of the boxes they hold, and nothing for the others. So nobody can spend another holder's days. A claim lists its box numbers in public, so the app never lists only yours: it claims for whole rows of ten numbers (0 to 9, 10 to 19, and so on), always the same rows, one transaction per row. Anyone watching learns at most that you may hold one of those ten. The purr halves every year, and the reserve pays a whole claim or none of it. Nobody but the claimer sees how much arrived.

The rats you adopt in the studio earn croquettes too, but not from the Pantry: each one gets 3 plain CROQ a day from the rats' own pantry, collected from "My rats", 7 days at most between two collections. Plain, not confidential: who owns a rat is public, so what it earns may be. That pantry got 500,000 CROQ from the treasury; the game reserve that feeds the boxes is not touched.
Croquettes go from the reserve to players and from players into their cats; every meal is split between the treasury, the reserve and the fire
Every croquette in the Pantry sits in exactly one encrypted pile: the reserve, the treasury's share, or the burnt one. A meal leaves nothing in the cat but weight. Burnt croquettes stay locked in the Pantry; no function can move them, and nobody can read how many there are.

Only the holder feeds their cat: at most 2 meals and 1,000 croquettes a day, however they are spread. Who holds the cat, how many meals it had today and the amount are all checked under encryption: a meal past the limits, or from someone who does not hold the cat, moves 0, silently. An offer past what is left of the day is cut down to it. Your browser encrypts the amount and the cat eats it all: its weight goes up by that much, encrypted, and nobody can read it while the box is sealed, the holder included. The croquettes are split: 20% to the collection's treasury, 60% back to the reserve that pays the purr, 20% burnt. Nobody can read the treasury's share between collections, the treasury included: read after each meal, it would tell who fed which cat and how much. It is sent to the treasury at most once every 7 days. If you hold less than you offered, the meal moves nothing, with no error and no hint. The meal itself is public and names the feeder, and the app only feeds cats you hold, so a meal shows that you hold that cat.

Once the box is opened, anyone can weigh the cat: its weight is decrypted in public and sets its build. Each cat also has a tolerance of its own, drawn from its seed. Nobody can know it while the seed is encrypted, and once it is public the cat has stopped eating. Weighed at or past it, the cat is sick: an ultra-rare trophy, never a death.
Build | Croquettes eaten | Days at the daily cap | Score
Thin | 0 – 0 | – | +0
Normal | 1 – 9,999 | 1 | +0
Chubby | 10,000 – 49,999 | 10 | +100
Fat | 50,000 – 149,999 | 50 | +300
Huge | 150,000+ | 150 | +700
Sick (a limit of its own) | 300,000 – 600,000 | 300 – 600 | +2000
The weight follows the box, and so does its stash. A buyer knows nothing of its meals: not how many, not how much, and not how close it is to its tolerance. The seller at least knows what they served themselves. The market prices the rest.

Nobody can read a weight before the box is opened, the holder included, for the same reason nobody is ever allowed on a seed: an access grant cannot be taken back, so a past holder would keep reading it after a sale. What stays secret, and what does not:
Fact | Who can read it
Your cCROQ balance | You
The amount of a transfer, a meal or a claim | The two sides of it
A cat's weight | Nobody while the box is sealed. Everyone once the cat is weighed
How much has been burnt | Nobody
Who tried to feed which cat | Everyone, and since the app only feeds your own cats, that you hold it. Whether it counted: only the feeder
Who claimed, and for which boxes | Everyone, but the app claims ten box numbers in a row at a time, so not which of them are yours. How much: only them
How heavy an opened cat came out, and whether it is sick | Everyone

Wrapping, unwrapping, market trades | Everyone, amounts included
The total supply | Everyone. How much still circulates: nobody
The treasury's share of the meals | Nobody, the treasury included. It is collected at most once every 7 days
There is no official price. Their value shows up indirectly, in what a heavy sealed cat sells for.
The public market is a Uniswap pool where CROQ trades against USDC. The collection put only croquettes in it, no dollars, so they sell from 0.001 USDC each upward, and never for less: selling only gives back the USDC that buyers brought. Until someone has bought, there is nothing to sell into, and the bureau de change says so. The pool's croquettes are locked in it for good: nobody can take them out, the collection included. Each trade pays the pool a 1% fee, which goes to the collection's treasury.

The studio is a page of its own, open to anyone, wallet or not: there you draw one of the depot's rats yourself. Rats, not cats, on purpose: the cats only come out of boxes, so nothing drawn in the studio can be taken for one. The button Another rat asks the game's own rat generator for a random one, in your browser: procedural, free, endless, and in 3D, turned with a drag. Buck teeth, big ears, a hat or a wedge of cheese, as the seed falls. No AI and nothing on-chain.
The studio's road, step by step, across your browser, the studio's server with the AI, and the chain
A random rat skips the AI: from step 1 it can go straight to adoption. An AI rat takes every step. Your words and drawings stay with the studio's server; only the pack and the adoption go on-chain.
1 Another rat Random, free, endless. No AI Your browser
2 Buy a pack 2 or 8 USDC, to the treasury On-chain

3 Sign in A free signature, no transaction Your browser
4 Sketch One unit: a picture from your words Studio and AI
5 3D model One unit, a minute or two Studio and AI
6 Adopt 1 USDC a random rat, 3 an AI rat On-chain
7 My rats 3 CROQ a day, and sniffing On-chain
Drawing a rat from your own words goes through paid AI services, so it is sold first, in packs bought on-chain in plain USDC from the StudioPacks contract: the Starter pack, 2 USDC for 10 sketches and one 3D model, and the Litter, 8 USDC for 50 sketches and five 3D models. The payment goes straight to the collection's treasury and the units never expire. A purchase is public, like any plain USDC payment; what you draw with it is not on-chain.

A sketch is one cartoon picture of your rat, drawn by the AI from what you wrote inside a fixed style, so it always comes out in the depot's look. It is cheap: try again until the rat looks right. A 3D model turns one of your sketches into a mesh that the page draws with the game's toon shading and outline, breathing slowly on the turntable. It takes a minute or two. A switch at the top of the page goes from the free random rats to the AI desk. A sketch shows up big on the drawing board, and you turn it into 3D from there. While the AI works, a rat runs in its wheel over a progress bar; you can leave the page, the work goes on, and the bar is back where it was when you return.

To spend your units, sign in once with your wallet: a free signature, no transaction, that tells the studio which units are yours. The site spends a unit before it calls the AI and gives it back if the service fails, up to three times a day: past that, or when the AI's safety checker refuses the picture, the unit is spent, since the service was paid. A prompt is 3 to 240 characters; licensed characters and adult content are refused before anything is spent. Each day the studio stops at a spending cap: past it, come back tomorrow.
On the testnet the USDC is pretend money while the AI costs real money, so the AI studio may be closed or kept to a list of testers there (the "Draw with AI" tab is then greyed out, and a tester opens it by signing in with their wallet); the random rats stay free everywhere.

A rat you like in the studio can be adopted: minted as an NFT of your own in the Rats contract, paid in plain USDC straight to the collection's treasury. A random rat costs 1 USDC and is adopted by its seed, each seed once: its look is worked out from that number again wherever it is shown, so there is nothing else to store. An AI rat costs 3 USDC: its picture is first stored on Arweave for good, like the cats' pictures, while its 3D model is kept by the game's server.
There will only ever be 700 random rats and 300 AI rats, set for good in the contract, and one wallet adopts 5 at most, both kinds together. A rat can still be given or sold to a wallet past that. The studio and the home page show how many are left.
One of the 700 random rats there will ever be, drawn in your browser from a random seed. Click it and another one lands.

A rat is everything a box is not, on purpose: the cats are the depot's secret residents, the rats its open ones. Who owns a rat and what it looks like are public, so it works like any NFT. It keeps one secret only: its power, below.
| A box | A rat
What it is | A sealed box with a cat nobody can see | A cartoon rat, there for anyone to see
Who holds it | Encrypted: only the holder knows | Public, like any NFT
What it is made of | One encrypted seed, readable by the contract only | Its seed, or its picture on Arweave, in the clear
Its secret | The cat, who holds it, what it earns | Its power (1, 2 or 3), read by its holder only
Price | 5 cUSDC, encrypted payment | 1 USDC, 3 for an AI rat, plain payment
How many | 10,000; how many are sold is encrypted | 700 random and 300 AI, 5 per wallet
Earns | A bag of 100 cCROQ, then 0 to 4 a day, hidden in the box | 3 plain CROQ a day, to its owner
Wallets and markets | Need a market built for the confidential ERC-721, like the flea market | A standard ERC-721: any wallet or market can show it

passages.heading: A rat's croquettes
passages.text:
Each rat earns 3 plain CROQ a day from the day it was adopted. They come from the rats' own pantry, the RatPantry, which got 500,000 CROQ from the treasury, and not from the Pantry that feeds the boxes: the rats never touch the game reserve. Collect them from "My rats" in the game, for all your rats at once. A rat keeps 7 days at most between two collections; left alone longer, it earns nothing more. If the pantry is ever empty, collecting fails and the days wait; when it runs low, it pays what is left. The croquettes are plain because a rat's owner is public anyway: there is nothing to hide in what it earns. Sealed at the bureau de change, they can feed a cat.
A rat's croquettes go from the treasury to the rats' pantry, from there to the rat's owner, and sealed, into a cat

passages.heading: A rat's croquettes
passages.text:
The rats' pantry is separate from the boxes' one: what the rats earn never comes out of the purr. Plain until you seal them, a rat's croquettes become secret the moment they enter cCROQ.
Treasury 500,000 CROQ, once
funded Rats' pantry 3 CROQ a rat a day
collect, 7 days at most You plain CROQ, in public
seal, then feed Your cat a meal, encrypted

passages.heading: A secret power
passages.text:
Every rat gets a secret power when it is adopted, random or AI, bought or given: 1, 2 or 3, drawn under encryption, so nobody, the team included, can choose or predict it. Only its holder can read it: in "My rats", press Read it. If you buy a rat, the first reading asks your wallet once for the right to read it; the seller keeps knowing what it was.
The three powers a rat can have, how often each comes, and what each does
Drawn at adoption, encrypted, readable by the rat's holder only.
Power | Sniffing a box | Set on a box
1 · Keen nose 55 rats in 100 | 2.5 cUSDC, 0.75 back in secret | Nothing: a bluff
2 · Trait jammer 30 rats in 100 | 2.5 cUSDC | Blocks the one trait you pick
3 · Total jammer 15 rats in 100 | 2.5 cUSDC | Blocks all five traits

passages.heading: Sniffing the boxes
passages.text:
A rat also sniffs. In "My rats", type the number of a sealed box you do not hold and press Sniff: your rat tells you one of its traits, for your eyes only. It is a paid shake, 2.5 cUSDC: 70% waits in the box for its holder, 30% goes to the treasury, and everyone else only sees that a rat sniffed that box. A power-1 rat gets 0.75 cUSDC of it back from the treasury, in secret: nobody can tell which rats sniff cheaper.
That is how a rat helps before a purchase: a few sniffs of a box you are thinking of buying, and you know as much about it as the seller did.

passages.heading: Protect or attack a box
passages.text:
A rat can also be set on a sealed box for 3 days; then it rests 7 days before it can go again. Type the box's number in "My rats", pick the trait to block (it only counts for a power-2 rat), and set it on the box. What it does depends on whose box it is, and the contract works that out by itself, in secret:
What a rat set on a box does, depending on whose box it is
On the chain every trick reads the same: a rat, a box, a date. Protect or attack, the power and the trait stay encrypted.
Where you set it | For 3 days | Who notices
On your own box | Strangers who shake or sniff it read a fake for the blocked traits | Nobody: the fake looks real
On someone else's box | Its holder's shakes of the blocked traits come back scrambled | The holder, that someone jams them. Not who
Either, with a power-1 rat | Nothing | Nobody: it looks like the others

passages.heading: Protect or attack a box
passages.text:
On one of your own boxes, it protects it. Whoever pays to shake it, or sends a rat to sniff it, reads a fake for the traits your rat blocks: the same fake every time, so it looks real. You still read the truth. Before a sale, that keeps your box's best traits to yourself.
On someone else's box, it attacks it. When its holder shakes their own box, the traits your rat blocks come back scrambled for 3 days. They learn that someone jams them, never who. A box protected by a power-3 rat resists attacks.
Every rat has the same button, the same 3 days and the same rest, so the chain only shows "rat 12 sat on box 340": not whether it protected or attacked, not its power, not which trait. A power-1 rat set on a box does nothing at all: a perfect bluff. Duels are not affected: the trait a loser shows is always the true one.

The flea market sits behind the depot, open after hours. Players sell each other sealed boxes, cats (boxes already opened) and rats, paid in cUSDC. Open it from the menu: Flea market. Each item hangs under a striped awning with its price tag, and three big buttons wait at the entrance: Mint a box takes you to the shelf for a brand new one, Mint a rat to the studio, and Sell to your own stall.

There are two ways to buy. The first is the price on the tag, which is public, and it takes two steps. Buy pulls the price from your cUSDC, all or nothing: what reaches the market is the whole price or zero, encrypted, so your balance stays sealed. Then one bit, paid or not, is decrypted in public and carried back on-chain with its proof, and the market settles. If you paid and the item is still as it was listed, it is yours. If someone else's purchase settled first, or the seller retagged it or took it back, you get back exactly what left your wallet. If your cUSDC did not cover the price, nothing was taken.

The second is a secret offer. Write an amount and press Seal it: your browser encrypts it, and the market holds it in escrow. Only you and the seller can ever read it; everyone else only sees that an offer was made. The seller breaks the seals, one signature for every offer on the stall, and may accept one at once: the item goes to you, the escrow to the seller, and that price is never published. An offer from a wallet that could not cover it holds zero, and the seller sees that. Until it is accepted you can take your offer back at any time, even after the listing is gone. The figure in How things come out plays both ways, step by step.
| At the asking price | With a secret offer
The price | Public, on the tag | Sealed: only you and the seller read it
How it goes | Buy, then one bit decrypted in public | Seal it, then the seller accepts when they like

If your cUSDC falls short | Nothing is taken | The offer holds zero, and the seller sees it
If you change your mind, or lose the race | Beaten to it, or the listing changed: refunded in full | Take it back any time until it is accepted
What everyone sees | That you bought it, and the price | That an offer was made, then that you bought it; never the price
Whichever way an item sells, 2.5% of the price goes to the depot and the rest to the seller. The contract can never set that cut above 10%.

passages.heading: A box keeps its state on the table
passages.text:
A box is sold in the public state it was listed in: sealed or opened, entangled or not, vet checked or not. If that changes while it is on sale, say its entangled partner is opened and opens it too, buying it or accepting an offer on it is refused, and a purchase still pending is refunded.
A sealed box on a table can still be sniffed: a paid shake tells you one of its traits, for your eyes only, as with any box. The holder's share of what you paid waits in the box as usual, and whoever buys the box collects it. Before buying a sealed box, assume the seller has shaken it; a few sniffs level that.

To sell, press Sell, pick a box, a cat or a rat, and set a price. The page shows what you get once the depot's 2.5% is taken, and buyers may also slip you sealed offers. Your boxes are known only to you, so finding them takes one signature to read your receipts, as Show my boxes does.
A rat is a plain NFT: it goes to the market and is listed at once. A box is not so simple, since nobody can check who holds it, the market included. So it goes to the market in a maybe transfer, like any gift, and whether it arrived is then decrypted in public. Only if it did does the listing open, so only a box's real holder can sell it, and once the market holds it nobody else can list it. Until then it shows as On its way.

Selling is a public act: selling a box shows everyone that you held it. What is inside stays sealed, for you as for the buyer. The seller of each listing, its asking price, the buyer of each sale, and whether each buyer at the asking price could pay are public. Balances, offer amounts and the price of a sale by offer never are.
While an item is on sale, Retag changes its price (purchases pending at the old price are refunded), and Take it back brings it home. Buyers keep their sealed offers to take back.
The flea market is open on Sepolia, with test dollars. In the demo, the night shift keeps a few stalls, slips a secret offer onto whatever you put on sale, and takes any offer worth at least 70% of your asking price.

The sealed vault is not part of the game: it lends the game's encryption to NFTs you already own. Put in an NFT of a collection the vault takes (on the testnet, a free test NFT) and you get a sealed box in exchange, an NFT of its own whose holder is encrypted, like the game's boxes. From then on nobody can tell who holds it: not the marketplaces, not the trackers, not the depot. The NFT stays in the vault until the box's holder takes it out, sells it on Seaport, or sells the box privately. Open it from the site's header: Vault.

Everything that leaves the vault is asked with the box's key, never with your address. The key is a secret your wallet makes from one free signature, the first time you use the vault in a session; nothing is stored, and the same wallet makes the same key on any device. It travels encrypted and tied to the exact request, so whoever carries it can neither read it, change where the NFT goes, nor use it again. The vault compares it with the box's key without decrypting either, and only one bit becomes public: the key matched, or not. A wrong key does nothing. Since any wallet can carry a request, the site's relayer sends yours: your address appears in none of them. Without a relayer, your wallet sends them, and its address shows. Sign that message only on DO NOT OPEN: whoever has the signature can take your NFTs out. The figure in How things come out plays a request step by step.

To sell in public, List on Seaport puts up a real Seaport order, the protocol OpenSea runs on, with the vault as the seller. Buyers see the NFT and the price, never who is selling, and any Seaport marketplace can fill it. While it is listed, the box stays put. Once a buyer pays, the ETH waits in the box for whoever holds its key; Collect the ETH sends it to any address, a fresh one if you like. Take the listing down, or let it run out, and the box is sealed again. On the testnet, OpenSea's own website may not show these listings; the orders are real all the same.

To sell to one person, Sell privately names a buyer and a price in cUSDC that only the buyer and you can read. If the buyer pays it in full while you still hold the box, the box, its key and the money change hands in one go; if not, nothing moves and the buyer gets everything back. Nothing about it is decrypted in public, so nobody else can tell whether it went through. Give the box sends it like any gift; it arrives with a random key nobody knows, and the receiver makes it theirs with Make the key mine, one signature, before anything can leave it. A Seaport sale and a private sale each leave 2.5% to the depot; the contract can never take more than 10%.

passages.heading: What shows, and what does not
passages.text:
Public: who put each NFT in (sealing is an ordinary NFT transfer), the NFT inside each box, the Seaport listings and their buyers, and the address an NFT or a sale's ETH is sent to. Never public: who holds a box, its key, a private sale's price, and whether a private sale or a gift moved anything. Until the box changes hands once, whoever sealed it is its obvious holder. Taking an NFT or ETH out to an address with no history shows no link to you, though the timing still can.
The vault is on Sepolia, with free test NFTs to mint and the real Seaport. In the demo it runs in memory: the night shift keeps two boxes in it, one of them on Seaport, buys whatever you list after a short while, and takes any private sale you offer it.
Open the vault

This part goes away at mainnet.
The game runs on Sepolia, Ethereum's test network. Nothing here is worth money. The USDC is Zama's test token, free from the wallet slip or the bureau de change; the ETH for gas comes from a faucet; the croquette pool only exists so the market can be tried; and every price in this manual is a test price.

The mainnet allow list has 1,500 seats, first come, first served: a seat goes to each player who claims one, or who connects an X account on the boarding page, until none is left. Your points: 3 for each opponent you beat in a duel, 1 for each opponent you faced, 2 for each box you opened, up to 10 boxes. A wallet linked to your X boarding pass gets 5 more, and 3 more again once you joined the Discord server and ran /board there with the code the boarding page gives you. Each friend who boards from your referral link adds 2 more, up to 10 friends, once their pass holds a seat with a wallet linked. Each opponent counts once, however many times you meet, and duels between your own wallets count nothing. Claim your place from the leaderboard's Duels tab by signing with your wallet: it is free and sends no transaction, and it tells the game only that your address is asking. Sign again later to update your points; the best you ever had are kept, even if the test network starts over. Claimants are ranked by points; between equal points, the earlier claim goes first.

Every seat comes with a gift, set by your rank among the seated players when the list closes. Ranks 1 to 500 fly First class: 100 to 500 cCROQ, a sealed box and a rat. Up to rank 1,000, Business: 50 to 250 cCROQ and a box. Up to rank 1,500, Economy: 20 to 100 cCROQ and a rat. The croquettes are drawn at random under encryption: only your wallet can read how many. The box is minted free for you out of the boxes kept outside the sale, so a sold-out sale never empties a gift; the rat is a free one, its seed drawn at random. Both are public, like any box's first holder after a mint of one. A gift nobody collects is never minted. The gift is collected on mainnet, in one transaction from the same Duels tab, within 30 days of the list closing, by a wallet that claimed its place: a seat held only by an X account has no wallet to send it to.

sections.title: Ce qu'il y a dans une boîte
Le dépôt en un coup d'œil
Personne ne sait qui détient quoi
Les frais, et où ils vont
Tant qu'on est sur le testnet

passages.text:
DO NOT OPEN est une collection de 10 000 NFT sur Ethereum, construite avec le chiffrement de Zama. Chaque token est une boîte en carton. Quand une boîte est mintée, le contrat tire un nombre aléatoire pour elle et garde ce nombre chiffré. Le chat à l'intérieur, son état, ses cinq traits et sa rareté découlent tous de ce seul nombre. Qui détient chaque boîte est chiffré aussi.
Chiffré ne veut pas dire ici caché derrière un serveur ou révélé plus tard depuis une liste préparée par quelqu'un. Le nombre est un chiffré sur la chaîne dès l'instant où il existe. Le contrat peut quand même calculer avec : le comparer, en découper un morceau, lui ajouter quelque chose. Il le fait sans jamais le déchiffrer, c'est à ça que sert le chiffrement totalement homomorphe.

Le jeu consiste donc à choisir ce que vous voulez découvrir, et ce que ça vous coûte. Secouez une boîte et vous apprenez une chose sur elle, en privé. Ouvrez-la et tout le monde apprend tout, pour de bon.

Le jeu a cinq guichets. Une règle les sépare : ce qui touche à une boîte est chiffré, ce qui touche à un rat ne l'est pas. L'argent passe de l'un à l'autre au bureau de change, et le montant se voit à la frontière.
Les dollars achètent des boîtes, des packs du studio et des rats ; les boîtes et les rats gagnent des croquettes ; les croquettes nourrissent les chats. Chaque carte mène à son chapitre.

Chaque boîte contient l'un d'eux. Dix races, du tigré de tous les jours au glitch qu'on ne croise presque jamais ; quatre états, dont un seul vraiment réveillé ; et quelques surprises en prime. Fais tourner le plateau et dis bonjour. Et puis ceux que tu fabriques toi-même à coups de croquettes, du maigre à l'énorme, jusqu'au malade.
1 / 10

passages.heading: Tigré
passages.text:
Environ 1 boîte sur 5
Le classique. Des rayures, des opinions bien arrêtées, et la certitude que ta chaise est à lui.
Les chances sous chaque chat viennent directement des tables du jeu. Comment une boîte tombe sur l'un d'eux, c'est la section suivante.

La première fois que vous connectez un wallet, le jeu vous tend une décharge, le formulaire DNO-1 : les conditions de jeu, huit clauses courtes. Elles disent clairement dans quoi vous vous engagez. Les contrats sont un logiciel expérimental : personne ne les a audités, et un bug, une faille ou un piratage pourrait faire perdre ce que vous y mettez, sans que les créateurs en soient responsables, dans la mesure où la loi le permet. Le site n'est qu'une fenêtre : vos boîtes, vos chats et vos soldes vivent on-chain, donc si le site tombe en panne, vous ne perdez rien. Personne ne garde votre argent pour vous, rien n'est remboursé, et rien de tout cela n'est un investissement.

Vous paraphez chaque clause, d'un clic, puis vous signez avec votre wallet. La signature est gratuite et n'envoie aucune transaction : votre wallet affiche un message lisible qui nomme votre adresse, la version des conditions et une empreinte du texte anglais complet. Les traductions servent à la lecture ; c'est le texte anglais que vous signez. La signature est gardée comme preuve de votre accord, par le serveur du jeu quand il répond, et toujours dans votre navigateur. Sans wallet, rien n'est demandé : vous pouvez visiter tout le site, et le formulaire n'apparaît que lorsqu'un wallet qui ne l'a pas encore signé se connecte. Vous pouvez le fermer pour continuer à visiter, ou passer à un autre wallet depuis le formulaire ; toute action demandée ensuite (un mint, une secousse, un repas) le fait revenir tant qu'il n'est pas signé.

Chaque nouveau wallet signe une fois, et une nouvelle version des conditions se signe à nouveau avant de continuer à jouer. Pour relire le formulaire et voir votre signature, ouvrez le menu et choisissez Conditions de jeu. Sur le réseau de test, rien n'est signé : la décharge attend le mainnet, et un avis dit à la place ce qu'une mise à jour des contrats garde (tes points, ta place sur la whitelist, ton passe X).

Une boîte contient une seule graine de 64 bits. Ses bits sont découpés en sept champs. Seize décident si le chat est vivant, endormi, fantôme ou quantique. Cinq octets sont les cinq traits. Le dernier octet ne change que l'apparence du chat.
Chiffrée
Champs de la graine
Une graine scellée L'ouvrir 0x ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ???? Cosmétique Pièce Chose cassée Accessoire Humeur Race Tirage d'état Bits 0 à 15. Seize bits décident de l'état : vivant 70%, endormi 20%, fantôme 8.0%, quantique 2.0%. La vérification de vie les compare à 45 875 sous chiffrement et publie la réponse sur un bit. Un secouage ne peut jamais renvoyer ces bits. Sur la chaîne, elle reste comme ça : un chiffré qui ressemble à du bruit. Le contrat calcule dessus sans le déchiffrer. Tirer une autre graine

Garder un seul nombre chiffré au lieu de huit permet un mint bon marché. Tout le reste en est déduit quand une mécanique en a besoin : sous chiffrement tant que la boîte est scellée, en clair une fois la boîte ouverte. L'app lit une graine exactement comme le contrat, donc le chat que vous voyez est bien celui que détient la chaîne.
Le score de rareté est une somme pondérée : trois fois le tirage de race, le tirage d'humeur, deux fois le tirage d'accessoire, la chose cassée, la pièce, plus un bonus pour l'état. Un chat quantique part avec 1 000 points d'avance. Le score maximal possible est 3 040.

Le propriétaire de chaque boîte est chiffré, comme sa graine. Ce n'est pas comme ça que fonctionnent d'habitude les NFT : un NFT ordinaire dit publiquement qui le possède. Ici, rien ne le dit. Personne ne peut voir qui détient une boîte, ni compter les boîtes de quelqu'un. La collection suit un nouveau standard écrit pour ça, l'ERC-721 confidentiel.
Envoyer une boîte n'échoue jamais à cause de qui la détient. Si vous la détenez, elle part ; sinon, rien ne se passe. Dans les deux cas, l'expéditeur et le destinataire reçoivent un reçu chiffré qu'eux seuls peuvent lire, qui dit si la boîte a bougé, et tous les autres voient un transfert qui a peut-être eu lieu, ou peut-être pas. Vous retrouvez vos propres boîtes de la même façon : l'app lit les reçus qui vous nomment et les déchiffre, avec une signature par visite. C'est ce que fait Afficher mes boîtes.

Le mint repose sur la même idée. Il se paie uniquement en cUSDC, et votre navigateur chiffre le nombre de boîtes voulu. Vous choisissez aussi parmi combien d'ids de token cacher ce nombre, de 1 à 10, et ce choix est public. Les premiers ids, jusqu'à votre quantité, sont à vous ; les autres sont des boîtes vides qui n'appartiennent à personne, et de l'extérieur les deux se ressemblent. Plus d'ids cachent mieux la quantité et coûtent plus de gas. Un mint qui dépasserait le plafond, ou que votre solde cUSDC ne couvre pas, n'obtient rien et ne paie rien.

Le nombre de boîtes vendues est un compteur chiffré, plafonné à 9 000 sous chiffrement : sur les 10 000 boîtes, les 1 000 autres sont gardées pour les cadeaux de la whitelist, mintées gratuitement quand un wallet assis récupère son cadeau, jamais vendues. Seuls des paliers de la vente sont annoncés : 100, 500, 1 000, 2 500, 5 000, 7 500, 9 000, le dernier voulant dire épuisé. Les boîtes offertes ne comptent dans aucun. Chaque mint rend publique une seule réponse, oui ou non : le palier suivant est-il atteint ? Et n'importe qui peut l'annoncer.

Certaines choses restent visibles, c'est voulu. Un mint montre l'adresse de l'acheteur et combien d'ids il a créés, ce qui borne par le haut ce qu'il a acheté. Une tentative de transfert montre qui l'a envoyée et à qui, comme un peut-être. Et une action qui doit devenir publique (une ouverture, une vérification de vie, une boîte mise en duel, ou un duel ou une intrication qui aboutit) montre que celui qui l'a lancée détenait cette boîte à ce moment-là. Une tentative de quelqu'un qui ne la détenait pas se solde par un refus et ne montre rien de la boîte. Les croquettes en ajoutent une : l'app ne nourrit que les boîtes que vous détenez, donc un repas, dont l'événement nomme celui qui nourrit, montre une boîte que vous détenez, même si le contrat traite de la même façon le repas d'un inconnu. Les réclamations, non : l'app réclame toujours pour des rangées entières de dix numéros de boîte, les vôtres parmi d'autres.
C'est aussi pour ça que le classement ne range que les chats ouverts, et les joueurs qui les ont ouverts : une ouverture publie qui l'a faite, alors que qui détient une boîte scellée reste caché.

L'un de ces faits publics va plus loin. Une fois qu'une action a montré qu'une adresse détenait une boîte, le transfert suivant de cette boîte depuis cette adresse est forcément réel, pas un peut-être : on peut donc suivre la boîte jusqu'à son détenteur suivant, et de là plus loin encore. Quand vous donnez une boîte, vous pouvez cocher « Envoyer 3 leurres avec » : trois transferts de plus de la même boîte vers des adresses au hasard, qui ne déplacent rien mais ressemblent au vrai, envoyés dans un ordre aléatoire avec lui. Personne ne peut alors dire lequel a déplacé la boîte, ni même si l'un l'a fait. Chacun coûte du gas. Sans leurres, gardez une boîte hors de vue en la recevant, ou en la déplaçant, sur une adresse neuve dont vous ne vous servez jamais pour prouver quoi que ce soit.

Chaque chiffré a une liste d'accès. Pour la graine, cette liste n'a qu'une entrée : le contrat. Aucun détenteur n'y est jamais ajouté, parce qu'une adresse sur la liste pourrait demander au service de clés de déchiffrer la graine directement et court-circuiter le jeu.
Information | Le détenteur | Tous les autres

Tous les prix sont en cUSDC, l'USDC confidentiel de Zama : personne d'autre que toi ne lit ton solde ni ne suit tes paiements, et le montant payé est chiffré comme le reste. Un paiement cUSDC ne peut pas échouer on-chain : un solde trop court déplace simplement 0, et l'action ne fait alors rien. Un mint n'obtient aucune boîte, un secouage payant lit « pas à toi », une caresse n'ajoute rien, une ouverture est refusée. Payer depuis de l'USDC ordinaire veut dire convertir d'abord le prix exact en cUSDC, en public, et pour un mint ce montant trahit la quantité. Convertir un montant rond à l'avance, au bureau de change, ne trahit rien.

Les duels ont leur propre classement, dans l'onglet Duels du classement : des boîtes, pas des joueurs, par duels gagnés, puis par le moins de défaites. Les trois premières portent une rosette épinglée sur le devant de leur boîte, or, argent et bronze, comme dans une exposition féline. Une boîte peut monter sur le podium et rester scellée : le classement n'utilise que les gagnants et les perdants que chaque duel rend déjà publics, jamais qui détient la boîte.

Il y a deux sorties du chiffrement. Un déchiffrement privé rechiffre une valeur pour une personne, qui doit figurer sur sa liste d'accès. Un déchiffrement public publie une valeur avec les signatures des parties qui se partagent la clé, et le contrat vérifie ces signatures avant de croire quoi que ce soit.
Le contrat ne reçoit jamais de callback. Une révélation, c'est une demande sur la chaîne, un déchiffrement hors chaîne, et une seconde transaction qui rapporte la preuve. N'importe qui peut envoyer cette seconde transaction. Chaque demande vérifie aussi, sous chiffrement, que celui qui la fait détient la boîte ; ce bit est déchiffré avec le reste, et un non solde la demande par un refus, avec des zéros à la place des valeurs de la boîte.

Sur ce protocole, un droit d'accès ne peut pas être révoqué. Une conception qui mettrait le détenteur sur la liste d'accès de la graine ne pourrait jamais en retirer le vendeur. Celle-ci n'y met jamais personne, donc une vente n'a rien à défaire sur la graine. Ce qui change de mains, c'est le propriétaire chiffré, avec ce qui attend dans la boîte : les gains des secouages payants et les croquettes la suivent.
Mint Graine : le contrat seulement. Propriétaire : Alice, chiffrée. Le reçu : Alice seulement.
Alice secoue Un nouveau chiffré contenant un trait : le contrat et Alice.
Alice vend à Bob Elle l'envoie. Le propriétaire change sous chiffrement, et le reçu, déplacé ou non, n'est lisible que par Alice et Bob. Rien ne change pour la graine.
Bob secoue Un autre nouveau chiffré : le contrat et Bob.

Alice réessaie Pas d'erreur. Elle lit « pas à toi » ; tous les autres voient un secouage, pas qu'il a échoué. Elle garde ce qu'elle a déjà vu, et n'obtient rien de nouveau.
Bob récupère Les gains des secouages payants et les croquettes qui attendent dans la boîte vont à lui maintenant, plus à Alice.
Si vous achetez une boîte scellée, partez du principe que le vendeur connaît ses cinq traits. Quelques secouages payants avant d'acheter rétablissent l'équilibre. Et un transfert qui vous nomme n'est qu'un peut-être tant que vous n'avez pas déchiffré son reçu : Afficher mes boîtes le fait pour vous.

Pourquoi les déchiffrements coûtent quelque chose : lire une valeur chiffrée demande du travail au réseau de Zama. Les parties qui se partagent la clé de déchiffrement doivent chacune y prendre part, et Zama le facture, pour chaque valeur lue, d'un dixième de centime à dix centimes selon la formule. Vérifier la preuve qui accompagne une valeur chiffrée par votre navigateur coûte cinq fois plus. Il le facture à la collection, pas à vous. Secouer, retrouver vos boîtes, lire votre propre solde, le résultat d'un duel : chacun est un déchiffrement. Minter, nourrir un chat ou envoyer des croquettes : chacun chiffre une valeur.

Chaque wallet a donc droit à 25 unités gratuites par jour, payées par la collection, et elles reviennent à minuit UTC ; un wallet qui n'a pas encore joué en a 16, de quoi faire un premier mint. Lire une valeur coûte une unité : un secouage en utilise 2, et retrouver les boîtes d'un mint en utilise une par numéro de boîte parmi lesquels il les a cachées. Chiffrer une valeur, comme la quantité d'un mint ou un repas, en coûte 5. Ce que votre navigateur a lu une fois, il s'en souvient, et ce n'est jamais compté à nouveau. Au-delà des gratuites, vous dépensez des crédits, un par unité, achetés au bureau de change. Leur prix suit ce que Zama facture à la collection en dollars, pas le cours du jeton de Zama : il ne bouge pas avec le marché. Ils se paient en USDC non chiffrés, exprès : un solde trop court annule l'achat, là où un paiement en cUSDC ne déplacerait rien, sans bruit. Rendre une valeur publique, pour ouvrir une boîte, régler un duel ou annoncer un palier, coûte 1 unité par valeur, comptée au portefeuille qui la demande en premier : une ouverture en prend 2 à 5, un duel 1 pour le poser et 5 pour le régler. Redemandée ensuite, par n'importe qui, elle est gratuite. Ainsi, personne ne peut poser des duels en boucle aux frais de la collection. Dans le jeu, le compteur Déchiffrements en haut à droite montre ce qu'il reste (gratuits du jour, plus crédits) : il clignote quand vous arrivez au bout, passe au rouge à zéro, et un clic ouvre le bureau de change pour en racheter.

La trésorerie paie ce qui fait tourner le jeu : les frais de Zama pour chaque unité gratuite, et les serveurs qui suivent la chaîne pour que le site reste rapide. Le reste va au projet. Personne ne peut lire les cUSDC qu'elle reçoit, propriétaire compris : lus après chaque paiement, ils trahiraient la quantité cachée de chaque mint, et donc qui a acheté quelles boîtes. Le propriétaire les retire au plus une fois tous les 7 jours, et n'apprend donc jamais que des sommes hebdomadaires. Les frais de 1 USDC d'une ouverture attendent qu'elle se règle : ils rejoignent la trésorerie quand la boîte s'ouvre, et reviennent à celui qui l'ouvrait si la boîte intriquée avec elle l'a ouverte d'abord.

Le jeu utilise cinq jetons : l'ETH pour le gas du réseau, l'USDC et le CROQ, en clair, et le cUSDC et le cCROQ, la même monnaie scellée. Un solde en clair est public, comme n'importe quel jeton ; un solde scellé est chiffré, et toi seul peux le lire. Pour passer de l'un à l'autre, ouvre le menu et choisis Bureau de change : dis ce que tu donnes et ce que tu veux, il trouve le chemin et affiche chaque coût avant que tu signes. Le taux et le nombre de transactions restent sous le formulaire ; Détails déplie le trajet, chaque frais et ce qui devient public. Il liste aussi ce que tu détiens ; les soldes scellés se déchiffrent à la demande, pour toi seul, en une signature.
Les cinq jetons du bureau de change : ETH, USDC et CROQ sont classiques, cUSDC et cCROQ scellés, et les chemins entre eux

Chaque flèche est une transaction ; toute autre paire les enchaîne, ETH vers cCROQ en trois. L'ETH peut aussi arriver directement en cUSDC par la rampe. Chaque passage de la frontière montre son montant ; du côté scellé, rien ne se voit.

Certains échanges tiennent en une transaction : acheter de l'USDC avec de l'ETH (il peut arriver scellé, en cUSDC), convertir de l'USDC en cUSDC ou l'inverse (Shield et Unshield), acheter ou vendre du CROQ contre de l'USDC, sceller du CROQ en cCROQ ou le desceller. Toute autre paire enchaîne ces étapes : de l'ETH au cCROQ, par exemple, il y en a trois. Chaque étape est une transaction à part, signée l'une après l'autre, et entre deux l'argent attend dans ton wallet en USDC ou en CROQ en clair. Si une étape ne livre rien, parce qu'un solde scellé plus petit que le montant ne déplace rien, sans un mot, le bureau s'arrête et te dit où est ton argent. L'ETH se donne seulement, il ne se reçoit jamais.

Acheter de l'USDC avec de l'ETH coûte 0,3 % de l'ETH, gardés par le site. Shield et Unshield sont gratuits. Chaque étape paie le gas du réseau, comme toute transaction. Un échange sur un pool peut se faire à un prix moins bon que celui annoncé si quelqu'un passe avant : la tolérance de slippage, 1 % sauf si tu la changes (de 0,01 % à 50 %), est l'écart que tu acceptes avant que la transaction s'annule d'elle-même, en ne coûtant que le gas. Le bureau montre aussi l'impact sur le prix, de combien ton propre échange fait bouger le prix du pool, et te prévient au-delà de 2 %.

Ce qui devient public : les jetons en clair circulent à découvert, donc chaque échange montre ses montants, comme chaque passage entre en clair et scellé. Le montant que tu convertis en cUSDC ou scelles est public, et celui que tu ramènes en clair aussi : il est déchiffré en public pour être versé, c'est pourquoi ces étapes prennent une minute de plus. Une fois ton argent scellé, ce que tu en fais reste privé.

Les crédits de déchiffrement s'achètent seulement en USDC en clair. Alors quand tu veux du cUSDC, depuis de l'ETH ou de l'USDC, le bureau peut en garder une part en clair : rien, 5 %, 10 % ou 20 %, et il retient ton choix. Depuis l'ETH, cela fait deux achats sur la rampe, un en clair et un scellé, aux mêmes frais ; depuis l'USDC, seul le reste est converti en cUSDC. Le bureau affiche l'USDC gardé et le nombre minimum de crédits qu'il achète. Les crédits eux-mêmes s'achètent seulement au bureau, dans un guichet à part à gauche du comptoir (sous tes avoirs sur un écran étroit), puisqu'ils se dépensent au lieu de se garder : tu choisis une quantité, tu vois le prix, tu achètes. S'il manque de l'USDC en clair, il te renvoie au comptoir pour en obtenir.

Les croquettes sont la monnaie du jeu, et elles existent sous deux formes. CROQ est un ERC-20 ordinaire avec une offre fixe de 20 000 000 : rien ne peut en créer d'autres, et il n'a pas de décimales, donc un CROQ vaut une croquette. Comme il est ordinaire, n'importe quel marché peut le lister. cCROQ est la même croquette emballée dans un jeton confidentiel (ERC-7984) : les soldes et les montants des transferts sont chiffrés. Le jeu n'utilise que cCROQ.
Le CROQ ordinaire s'échange sur un marché public ; emballé, il devient le cCROQ confidentiel, celui du jeu
Passer la frontière montre le montant : emballer déplace du CROQ ordinaire, et déballer passe par un déchiffrement public. Tout ce qui se passe en cCROQ entre les deux reste chiffré.
Toute l'offre a été créée une seule fois, au déploiement, et répartie ainsi :

Les croquettes arrivent aux joueurs par le Garde-manger, le contrat qui gère l'économie. Chaque boîte achetée apporte un sac de bienvenue de 100 à sa première réclamation : une fois par boîte, quel que soit son détenteur, donc un second wallet ne rapporte rien. Ensuite chaque boîte ronronne : chaque jour, un montant chiffré entre 0 et 4, multiplié par 2 pour une boîte Vet Certified, à récupérer jusqu'à 7 jours d'un coup. Un id vide, de ceux qu'un mint crée au-delà de la quantité achetée et que personne ne détient, n'a ni sac ni ronron. Sacs et ronrons sont versés dans la boîte, une réserve chiffrée, et celui qui réclame reçoit les réserves des boîtes qu'il détient, et rien pour les autres. Personne ne peut donc dépenser les jours d'un autre détenteur. Une réclamation liste ses numéros de boîte en public, donc l'app ne liste jamais seulement les vôtres : elle réclame pour des rangées entières de dix numéros (0 à 9, 10 à 19, etc.), toujours les mêmes, une transaction par rangée. Qui regarde apprend au plus que vous détenez peut-être l'une de ces dix. Le ronron est divisé par deux chaque année, et la réserve paie une réclamation entière ou rien du tout. Personne d'autre que celui qui réclame ne voit combien il a reçu.

Les rats que vous adoptez dans le studio gagnent aussi des croquettes, mais pas dans le Pantry : chacun reçoit 3 CROQ classiques par jour du garde-manger des rats, à récolter depuis « Mes rats », 7 jours au plus entre deux récoltes. Classiques, pas confidentielles : le propriétaire d'un rat est public, ce qu'il gagne peut l'être aussi. Ce garde-manger a reçu 500 000 CROQ de la trésorerie ; la réserve du jeu qui nourrit les boîtes n'est pas touchée.
Les croquettes vont de la réserve aux joueurs et des joueurs à leurs chats ; chaque repas est partagé entre la trésorerie, la réserve et le feu

Chaque croquette du Garde-manger est dans exactement un tas chiffré : la réserve, la part de la trésorerie, ou le tas brûlé. Un repas ne laisse rien dans le chat, sauf du poids. Les croquettes brûlées restent bloquées dans le Garde-manger ; aucune fonction ne peut les déplacer, et personne ne peut lire combien il y en a.

Seul le détenteur nourrit son chat : au plus 2 repas et 1 000 croquettes par jour, quelle que soit la répartition. Qui détient le chat, combien de repas il a eus aujourd'hui et le montant sont tous vérifiés sous chiffrement : un repas qui dépasse les limites, ou servi par quelqu'un qui ne détient pas le chat, déplace 0, sans bruit. Une offre qui dépasse ce qui reste du jour est ramenée à ce reste. Ton navigateur chiffre le montant et le chat mange tout : son poids augmente d'autant, chiffré, et personne ne peut le lire tant que la boîte est scellée, détenteur compris. Les croquettes sont partagées : 20 % pour la trésorerie de la collection, 60 % retournent à la réserve qui paie le ronron, 20 % sont brûlés. Personne ne peut lire la part de la trésorerie entre deux collectes, trésorerie comprise : lue après chaque repas, elle dirait qui a nourri quel chat, et de combien. Elle lui est envoyée au plus une fois tous les 7 jours. Si tu en as moins que ce que tu offres, le repas ne déplace rien, sans erreur ni indice. Le repas lui-même est public et nomme celui qui le sert, et l'app ne nourrit que les chats que tu détiens : un repas montre donc que tu détiens ce chat.

Une fois la boîte ouverte, n'importe qui peut peser le chat : son poids est déchiffré publiquement et fixe sa corpulence. Chaque chat a aussi sa propre tolérance, tirée de sa graine. Personne ne peut la connaître tant que la graine est chiffrée, et quand elle devient publique le chat a fini de manger. Pesé à sa tolérance ou au-delà, le chat est malade : un trophée ultra rare, jamais une mort.
